cut.note: a library of classical AI mechanisms, each written twice (a first version and the version that fixes its documented failure): means-ends analysis with a goal stack; a pattern matcher whose operators are dispatched through symbol properties; unification with an occurs check and substitution; a Prolog compiler that turns clauses into Lisp functions in continuation-passing style with a trail; and a generic tree search parameterised by how new states are combined with the frontier. The cut takes the five as organs at inventory depth; each file is a specimen-sized body

organs.human_name: gps.lisp GPS / achieve-all / achieve / apply-op / appropriate-p (42-93); version 2: achieve-all with orderings, achieve-each, appropriate-ops sorted by unmet preconditions (202-243)
organs.mechanism: a goal holds if it is in the state; else, unless it is already on the goal stack (a loop), try each operator whose add list contains it: achieve the operator's preconditions recursively with the goal pushed on the stack, then apply it (delete its del list, append its add list); all goals must be achieved AND still hold at the end; version 2 tries the goals in the given and the reversed order and sorts candidate operators by how many preconditions are unmet (the Sussman-anomaly and 'leaping before you look' fixes the book documents)
organs.input: a state (a list of conditions), goals, operators
organs.output: a new state containing executed actions, or nil
assumptions: the world is a set of literals changed by add/delete lists (STRIPS); differences between state and goal select operators (Newell & Simon's GPS)
organs.fitness_value_in_ancestor: the first general problem solver, small enough to read; its failures (clobbered siblings, prerequisite loops, infinite regress) are named and reproduced in the same file
organs.failure_landscape: by reading: version 2's two orderings are not a complete search; the book says so

organs.human_name: patmatch.lisp pat-match (15), single-match / segment-match dispatch via (get symbol 'single-match) (32-40): ?is ?or ?and ?not ?* ?+ ?? ?if; segment-match with first-match-pos (110-136); rule-based-translator (169)
organs.mechanism: a pattern is matched against input with a binding list; variables (?x) bind or must agree; operator patterns are looked up by their leading symbol's property (single-match for predicates and Boolean combinations, segment-match for ?* and friends, which try successive split points of the input, shortest first, and backtrack by returning fail); rule-based-translator applies the first rule whose pattern matches and substitutes the bindings into a response (ELIZA)
organs.input: a pattern, an input list, bindings
assumptions: extending the matcher by adding a property to a symbol is the right extension mechanism (data-driven dispatch)
organs.fitness_value_in_ancestor: one matcher serves ELIZA, STUDENT and the rule systems in the book
organs.failure_landscape: by reading: segment matching is exponential in the number of segment variables
organs.human_prior: Weizenbaum 1966 (ELIZA); the atlas's eliza-weizenbaum-mad-slip-1965 cut found the original matcher (YMATCH/ASSMBL) outside its body: this file is the readable descendant

organs.human_name: unify.lisp unify / unify-variable / occurs-check / subst-bindings / unifier (11-60); *occurs-check* t
organs.mechanism: two terms unify if equal, or one is a variable (bind it after following existing bindings and, if enabled, checking the variable does not occur in the other term), or both are conses whose cars and cdrs unify in sequence with the bindings threaded through; substitution replaces bound variables recursively, reusing structure when nothing changes
assumptions: bindings as an association list are enough at this scale; the occurs check is a switch because Prolog omits it for speed
organs.fitness_value_in_ancestor: the core of the Prolog interpreter and compiler in the same book
organs.failure_landscape: by reading: without the occurs check, unifying ?x with (f ?x) builds a cyclic term

organs.human_name: prologc.lisp: prolog-compile / compile-clause / compile-call (66-107, 289-302); compile-unify / compile-unify-variable specialising unification at compile time (190-237); deref, unify!, set-binding!, undo-bindings! and the trail (14-64); top-level-prove, run-prolog
organs.mechanism: each predicate becomes a Lisp function taking its arguments and a continuation; each clause becomes a body that unifies the head arguments (with unification partly evaluated at compile time when a variable's status is known), calls the body goals with nested continuations, and undoes bindings on the trail before trying the next clause; variables are mutable structures set destructively (unify!) and dereferenced on read; the top level runs the goals with a continuation that prints solutions
assumptions: backtracking is cheapest as continuation calls plus a trail (the 'compile to the host language' route, not a WAM)
organs.fitness_value_in_ancestor: a Prolog compiler in a few hundred lines; the book's benchmark is zebra
organs.human_prior: Warren 1983 (WAM) as the rival design; the atlas's swipl-9.2.9 cut holds the WAM lineage

evidence.ref: vault:paip-lisp-norvig-1991/upstream/tree/lisp/prologc.lisp:14-345 (inventory; compile-unify read at the signature level)

organs.source_boundary: prologc.lisp; CANDIDATE because bodies were skimmed

organs.human_name: search.lisp tree-search (7); depth-first-search (prepend as combiner), breadth-first-search (append), best-first-search (sorter cost-fn), beam-search (sorter then truncate to beam-width) (19-68)
organs.mechanism: tree-search keeps a list of states; it pops the first, returns it if it satisfies the goal, else generates successors and combines them with the remaining states by a supplied function; the four searches differ only in that function: new states first (depth), last (breadth), merged and sorted by cost (best-first), or sorted and cut to a width (beam)
organs.input: a start state, goal predicate, successor function, combiner
assumptions: the frontier policy is the whole difference between the classical searches
organs.failure_landscape: by reading: no visited set (graph-search is a later section)

pressures.source_evidence: gps.lisp both versions and the examples in the file
pressures.condition: an organism has operators with preconditions and add/delete lists and a conjunctive goal; achieving one goal can undo another (the Sussman anomaly); a precondition can require the goal being pursued (a loop)
pressures.failure_condition: a returned state that does not satisfy all goals, or non-termination
pressures.world_punishes: achieving goals independently and not re-checking; no goal stack
pressures.world_rewards: a final subset check, a goal stack, ordering by unmet preconditions
pressures.observable_consequence: success on the blocks-world and monkey-and-bananas sets in the file (the book's test cases) for version 1 vs version 2
pressures.trivial_shortcuts: a complete planner (Graphplan, in this atlas)
pressures.cheat_control: an organism given the plan must reproduce the final state; version 1 must fail the Sussman anomaly where version 2 succeeds; both must fail the book's 'infinite regress' example (documented): the world must show all three
pressures.purpose_separated_from_pressure: PURPOSE: exposition of classical AI programs (Norvig 1991)
